sources.spo2: Analog: Harespod hypobaric chamber (Sci Data 2024), scaled per person, shown as 75-99 %
sources.hr: EV1: Harespod. EV2: NASA Flight Crew Physiological Data (ECG-derived)
sources.hrv: NASA Flight Crew Physiological Data for Crew State Monitoring (ECG-derived RMSSD)
sources.resp: NASA Flight Crew Physiological Data for Crew State Monitoring (ECG-derived breathing)
sources.suit: Simulated from NASA suit spec (4.3 psia, 100 % O2) and the replay's equivalent altitude
sources.reaction: Simulated here; measured live by the helmet HUD reaction check
sources.dcs_model: NASA TP-2014-218561 Hypobaric DCS Treatment Model (Conkin et al.)
sources.runtime: Browser-only demo build: the detector runs on this device

call.title: Voice check
call.prompt: Call {crew} on the loop: “{crew}, Habitat. State your O₂ reading.” How do they answer?
call.detail: Slurred speech, slow answers or wrong numbers are early hypoxia signs. Hypoxic crew often feel fine.

options.label: Clear and correct
options.sub: Answers quickly, reads the right value

options.label: No answer after 2 calls
options.sub: Or only noise on the loop

why.text: Procedural errors appear to increase at 3,048 m (10,000 ft) though manual control holds
why.source: NASA NTRS 20150021491, Risk of Hypobaric Hypoxia evidence report, p. 13

why.text: Crew must be trained to recognise their symptoms; avoid critical tasks and keep workload low during atmosphere transitions
why.source: NASA NTRS 20150021491, Risk of Hypobaric Hypoxia evidence report, p. 25

suit.title: Suit pressure check
suit.prompt: Look at {crew}'s suit pressure on the left: {suit} psia. Is it below 4.0 psia?
suit.detail: Nominal suit pressure is 4.3 psia with 100 % O₂. Lower pressure means less O₂ reaching the lungs.

sensor.title: Reaction check
sensor.prompt: Suit looks normal. Ask {crew} to stop, rest 30 s and press the HUD reaction check. What happens?
sensor.detail: A slipped forehead sensor can read low. A real drop shows up as a slow or missed reaction.

options.label: Fast reaction, SpO₂ recovers
options.sub: Likely sensor slip or heavy exertion

watch.title: Watch & reseat sensor
watch.prompt: Treat as a false alarm, but keep watching.
steps: Tell {crew} to reseat the comm cap so the forehead sensor sits flat.
Lower {crew}'s workload for 5 minutes.
If SpO₂ falls again, restart this response.

act_now.title: Emergency O₂ + buddy
act_now.prompt: Act now: get {crew} on emergency O₂ and send the buddy.
steps: Tell {crew}: “STOP work. Hold position. Check your tether.”
Tell {crew} to open the emergency (secondary) O₂ supply per suit procedure. If they can't, EV2 does it for them.
Send the other EVA crewmember to {crew}: check their display and helmet, stay in arm's reach.
Call flight surgeon / mission control: “Suspected hypoxia, {crew}, SpO₂ {spo2} %.”

why.text: Supplemental O2 should be available during decompressions and throughout the mission
why.source: NASA NTRS 20150021491, Risk of Hypobaric Hypoxia evidence report, p. 24

why.text: Hypoxia worsens judgement before the crewmember notices it, so the buddy checks instead of relying on self-report.

o2_effect.title: O₂ effect check
o2_effect.prompt: After 2 minutes on emergency O₂, what is {crew}'s SpO₂ doing? Now {spo2} %, baseline {base} %.

return.title: Return to airlock
return.prompt: Controlled return to the airlock. End the EVA for {crew}.
steps: {crew} and buddy walk back together; no carrying tools.
Prepare the airlock: O₂ mask with regulator, pulse oximeter, medical kit at the hatch.
Repress the airlock to habitat pressure (8.2 psia) as soon as both are in.

escort.title: Emergency escort
escort.prompt: Emergency return. Buddy brings {crew} in now.
steps: Buddy clips to {crew} and leads them back; {crew} does nothing but walk.
Keep talking to {crew} every 30 s; note any change in speech.
Prepare the airlock: O₂ mask, bag-valve mask, AED and medical kit at the hatch.
Start airlock repress the moment both are inside.

helmet.title: Helmet off, mask on
helmet.prompt: Get {crew} breathing cabin air and O₂.
steps: Check pressure is equal, then remove {crew}'s helmet.
Put on the O₂ mask: 100 % O₂, high flow.
Clip the pulse oximeter on a finger.

why.text: Supplemental O2 should be available during decompressions and throughout the mission
why.source: NASA NTRS 20150021491, Risk of Hypobaric Hypoxia evidence report, p. 24

o2_awake.title: Rest on O₂
o2_awake.prompt: Rest on O₂ and recheck in 5 minutes.
steps: Sit {crew} upright and keep them still: no tasks.
Keep 100 % O₂ flowing; check the mask seal.
Target SpO₂ 94 % or above.

o2_confused.title: Stay & monitor
o2_confused.prompt: Stay with {crew}. O₂ on, recheck in 5 minutes.
steps: Do not leave {crew} alone or let them operate anything.
Keep 100 % O₂ flowing; check the mask seal.
Call the flight surgeon now for a private medical conference.
Ask simple questions every 2 minutes and note the answers.

recovery.title: Recovery position
recovery.prompt: Protect the airway and get the flight surgeon.
steps: Lay {crew} on their side (recovery position), head tilted to keep the airway open.
Keep 100 % O₂ on by mask.
Emergency call to flight surgeon / mission control.
Check breathing every minute. If it stops, go to CPR.

cpr.title: CPR
cpr.prompt: Start CPR. This is a medical emergency.
steps: Call mission control: medical emergency, {crew}.
Start chest compressions: arms straight, shoulders over hands, 100–120 per minute; brace yourself against the floor.
Ventilate with the bag-valve mask on 100 % O₂.
Attach the AED and follow its voice prompts.

recheck.title: SpO₂ recheck
recheck.prompt: After 5 minutes on O₂, {crew}'s SpO₂ is…
recheck.detail: Live value: {spo2} %. Baseline before the EVA: {base} %.

escalate.title: Escalate
escalate.prompt: O₂ isn't working well enough. Check equipment and escalate.
steps: Check the O₂ supply is open and flowing; the mask bag should stay inflated.
Refit the mask; try the bag-valve mask if breathing is shallow.
Flight surgeon on the loop now. Consider other causes: DCS, CO₂, injury.

orient.title: Orientation check
orient.prompt: Ask {crew}: Where are you? What day is it? What's your crewmate's name? How many are correct?

dcs_screen.title: DCS screen
dcs_screen.prompt: The EVA was at 4.3 psia, so check for DCS too. Does {crew} have joint pain, numbness, rash or chest tightness?
dcs_screen.detail: DCS can look like hypoxia, but it doesn't go away with O₂ alone.

dcs_link.title: Open DCS check
dcs_link.prompt: Possible DCS. Keep {crew} on 100 % O₂ and open the DCS check.
steps: Keep {crew} lying or sitting still on 100 % O₂.
Open the DCS check from the button below.

monitor.title: Monitor & hand off
monitor.prompt: Monitor and hand off to the flight surgeon.
steps: Keep O₂ on for 15 more minutes, then room air if SpO₂ stays at 94 % or above.
Check SpO₂ and alertness every 10 minutes for 30 minutes.
No further EVA for {crew} until the flight surgeon clears them.
Send the hand-off report from the Log tab.

why.text: Crew must be trained to recognise their symptoms; avoid critical tasks and keep workload low during atmosphere transitions
why.source: NASA NTRS 20150021491, Risk of Hypobaric Hypoxia evidence report, p. 25

end_ok.title: Response complete
end_ok.prompt: Response complete for {crew}. Every step is in the Log.

end_handover.title: Surgeon takes over
end_handover.prompt: Flight surgeon is leading care for {crew}. Steps so far are in the Log.

when.title: Symptom onset
when.detail: Decompression sickness (DCS) comes from nitrogen bubbles after going from habitat pressure (8.2 psia) to suit pressure (4.3 psia).

options.label: After coming back in
options.sub: NASA treats this as more serious

ts.title: Onset time
ts.prompt: How many minutes into the EVA did the first symptom appear?
ts.detail: Count from leaving habitat pressure. Used by NASA's treatment model below.

symptoms.title: Symptom map
symptoms.prompt: Ask and look. Which does {crew} have? Select all that apply.

options.label: Chest pain, cough, short of breath

why.text: Type I: joint pain, peripheral nerve symptoms or simple skin bends. Type II: central nervous system, circulation (collapse/shock) or lungs (the chokes); also unusual headache and inappropriate fatigue. Type II is serious DCS. Marbled skin is its own category.

none.title: No DCS signs
steps: Recheck {crew} at 30 minutes and 2 hours after the EVA.
Ask {crew} to report any new ache, tingling or rash straight away.

type1.title: Treat Type I
type1.prompt: Likely Type I DCS (mild). Treat now; it usually resolves.
steps: Give 100 % O₂ by mask.
Keep {crew} resting: no exercise, no moving the painful joint.
Give oral fluids, about 1 litre.
Rate the pain 0–10 and note where it is.
Symptoms first appeared after the EVA? NASA moves straight to the BTA.

cm.title: Treat marbled skin
cm.prompt: Marbled skin (cutis marmorata). It often comes with serious symptoms; treat promptly.
steps: Give 100 % O₂ by mask.
Keep {crew} lying still and check for any Type II signs every 5 minutes.
Call the flight surgeon now.

why.text: Cutis marmorata is often associated with serious Type II symptoms.

type2.title: Treat Type II
type2.prompt: Serious (Type II) DCS. Treat with pressure now and call the flight surgeon.
steps: Emergency call to flight surgeon / mission control.
Give 100 % O₂ by mask; lay {crew} flat.
Prepare {crew}'s suit and the Bends Treatment Apparatus (next screen).
If {crew} can't drink, IV normal saline 1 L/h from the medical kit, as the flight surgeon directs.

why.text: The ISS medical kit holds 4 L of normal saline; oral fluids first, IV saline at 1 L per hour if needed.

model.title: Treatment odds
model.prompt: How likely is each treatment to resolve {crew}'s symptoms?
model.detail: NASA's DCS treatment model, from 154 cases of altitude DCS. Uses the time the symptom appeared.

after.title: 10-min recheck
after.prompt: After 10 minutes on 100 % O₂ at habitat pressure, how are {crew}'s symptoms?

continue.title: 2 h on O₂
continue.prompt: Keep going: 2 hours of 100 % O₂ at habitat pressure.
steps: Keep {crew} resting on 100 % O₂ for 2 hours.
Check symptoms every 15 minutes; any new or worse symptom: go to the BTA.
Flight surgeon decides when {crew} can stop O₂.

why.text: 2 h of 100 % O₂ at 8.2 psia raised the chance of resolution to 0.99 in NASA's Mars EVA case.

bta.title: BTA pressurise
bta.prompt: Pressurise with the Bends Treatment Apparatus (BTA).
steps: {crew} dons the suit (helmet and gloves on) inside the habitat.
Fit the BTA and pressurise the suit to 8.0 psid above cabin.
Keep 100 % O₂ in the suit; stay on the loop with the flight surgeon.
Log the time pressurised. The suit can't be used for EVA again until recertified.

why.text: The BTA is used if DCS is serious, doesn't resolve with 100 % O₂, or first appears after the EVA. It lets the suit be pressurised to 8.0 psid above cabin.

monitor.title: Monitor & hand off
monitor.prompt: Monitor and hand off to the flight surgeon.
steps: Check symptoms every 15 minutes and log each check.
No EVA for {crew} until the flight surgeon clears them.
Send the hand-off report from the Log tab.

end_ok.title: Check complete
end_ok.prompt: DCS check complete for {crew}. Every step is in the Log.

dcs_options.label: Back in habitat
dcs_options.detail: Habitat at 8.2 psia, 100 % O₂ by mask

dcs_options.label: Suit + Bends Treatment Apparatus
dcs_options.detail: Suit pressurised 8.0 psid over the 8.2 psia habitat
